title: Renal Drug Clearance and Dosing

items.text: The kidney is a major route of elimination for many drugs and active metabolites — renal function directly determines how long a drug stays in the body.

emphasis.text: The kidney is a major route of elimination for many drugs and active metabolites — renal function directly determines how long a drug stays in the body.

items.md: **The kidney is a major route of elimination for many drugs and active metabolites — renal function directly determines how long a drug stays in the body.**

items.text: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and creatinine clearance (CrCl) are the standard measures used to estimate renal drug-elimination capacity.
items.md: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and creatinine clearance (CrCl) are the standard measures used to estimate renal drug-elimination capacity.

items.text: As GFR falls, renally cleared drugs accumulate — dosing must be adjusted by reducing the dose, extending the interval, or both.
items.md: As GFR falls, renally cleared drugs accumulate — dosing must be adjusted by reducing the dose, extending the interval, or both.

items.text: Examples of drugs requiring renal dose adjustment: most antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin, many beta-lactams), digoxin, many direct oral anticoagulants, metformin, and the diuretics covered later in this session.
items.md: Examples of drugs requiring renal dose adjustment: most antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin, many beta-lactams), digoxin, many direct oral anticoagulants, metformin, and the diuretics covered later in this session.

items.text: Renal impairment also raises drug-interaction risk — drugs that are individually safe can become dangerous in combination when renal clearance is already reduced (a theme that returns explicitly in Session 2's "triple whammy" discussion).

emphasis.text: Renal impairment also raises drug-interaction risk — drugs that are individually safe can become dangerous in combination when renal clearance is already reduced (a theme that returns explicitly in Session 2's "triple whammy" discussion).

items.md: **Renal impairment also raises drug-interaction risk — drugs that are individually safe can become dangerous in combination when renal clearance is already reduced (a theme that returns explicitly in Session 2's "triple whammy" discussion).**

notes:
This is foundational Chapter 3 content applied specifically to the renal unit — the goal is for students to see renal dosing not as a separate topic but as the lens through which every other drug in this unit (and this course) should be viewed.

Instructor script:

GFR and creatinine clearance estimate elimination capacity. As GFR falls, renally cleared drugs accumulate. Examples: vancomycin, many beta-lactams, digoxin, DOACs, metformin.

title: Loop Diuretics

items.text: Mechanism: block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb — the site responsible for ~25% of filtered sodium reabsorption.

emphasis.text: Mechanism: block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb — the site responsible for ~25% of filtered sodium reabsorption.

items.md: **Mechanism: block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb — the site responsible for ~25% of filtered sodium reabsorption.**

items.text: Furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide — used for edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, renal disease) and, at times, hypertension when a thiazide alone is insufficient (e.g., significant renal impairment).
items.md: Furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide — used for edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, renal disease) and, at times, hypertension when a thiazide alone is insufficient (e.g., significant renal impairment).

items.text: Adverse effects: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, ototoxicity (especially with rapid IV administration or high doses), and hyperuricemia.

items.md: **Adverse effects: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, ototoxicity (especially with rapid IV administration or high doses), and hyperuricemia.**

items.text: Furosemide carries a sulfonamide-related structure — historical cross-reactivity concern with sulfa allergy, though the clinical risk is now considered low; still worth a careful allergy history.

items.text: Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion — useful in hypercalcemia, and the opposite effect of thiazides (Figure 2 explains the mechanism).
items.md: Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion — useful in hypercalcemia, and the opposite effect of thiazides (Figure 2 explains the mechanism).

notes:
The calcium-handling difference between loops and thiazides is one of the highest-yield comparison points in this whole unit — make sure students can state it both ways (loops increase Ca2+ excretion, thiazides decrease it) before moving to Figure 2.

Instructor script:

Furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Most potent. Adverse effects: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, ototoxicity, hyperuricemia.

Know: Increase calcium excretion (useful in hypercalcemia). Sulfonamide allergy cross-reactivity is low.

title: Thiazide Diuretics

items.text: Mechanism: block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule — a less potent natriuretic site (~5–8% of filtered sodium) than the loop.

items.text: Hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone — first-line agents for essential hypertension; chlorthalidone has a longer half-life and is often preferred for 24-hour BP control.

items.text: Adverse effects: hyponatremia (can be significant, especially in older adults), hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia (can precipitate gout), and hypercalcemia.

items.text: Thiazides decrease calcium excretion (opposite of loop diuretics) — can be therapeutically useful in patients with osteoporosis and recurrent calcium-containing kidney stones.

items.text: Lose efficacy as GFR falls below approximately 30 mL/min — loop diuretics are generally preferred once renal function is significantly reduced.

notes:
The "thiazides lose efficacy in advanced CKD" point sets up a direct bridge to Session 2's hypertension-in-CKD content — flag that connection explicitly here.

Instructor script:

Block NCC in the distal tubule. First-line in hypertension. Adverse effects: hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, hypercalcemia. Lose efficacy at GFR below about 30.

items.text: Clinical pearl:  Thiazide diuretics lose much of their natriuretic efficacy once GFR falls below roughly 30 mL/min, because there is too little filtered sodium reaching the distal tubule for the drug to act on meaningfully. A loop diuretic, which acts upstream at the thick ascending limb, remains effective even in advanced CKD and is the more appropriate choice here.

title: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors & Osmotic Diuretics

items.text: ●  Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor): blocks Na+/HCO3- reabsorption in the proximal tubule; weak diuretic effect but valued for non-diuretic uses — glaucoma (reduces aqueous humor production), altitude sickness prophylaxis, and metabolic alkalosis correction. Causes a mild metabolic acidosis as a predictable adverse effect.
items.md: **●  Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor):** blocks Na+/HCO3- reabsorption in the proximal tubule; weak diuretic effect but valued for non-diuretic uses — glaucoma (reduces aqueous humor production), altitude sickness prophylaxis, and metabolic alkalosis correction. Causes a mild metabolic acidosis as a predictable adverse effect.

items.text: ●  Mannitol (osmotic diuretic): an inert, filtered but poorly reabsorbed solute that holds water in the tubule lumen osmotically. Used to reduce elevated intracranial or intraocular pressure and in certain cases of rhabdomyolysis-associated kidney injury prevention. Requires intact renal perfusion to be effective and can worsen volume overload if used inappropriately.
items.md: **●  Mannitol (osmotic diuretic):** an inert, filtered but poorly reabsorbed solute that holds water in the tubule lumen osmotically. Used to reduce elevated intracranial or intraocular pressure and in certain cases of rhabdomyolysis-associated kidney injury prevention. Requires intact renal perfusion to be effective and can worsen volume overload if used inappropriately.

notes:
Both of these classes are "know the niche use, not the everyday one" — students should walk away knowing acetazolamide = glaucoma/altitude sickness and mannitol = ICP/IOP reduction, more than thinking of either as a mainstream diuretic.

Instructor script:

Acetazolamide for glaucoma, altitude sickness and alkalosis. Mannitol for raised ICP and IOP.

title: The Hyperkalemia Setup

items.text: Clinical pearl:  Both the ACE inhibitor (by reducing aldosterone) and spironolactone (by directly blocking the aldosterone receptor) independently reduce potassium excretion — combined, and in the setting of CKD (which already impairs potassium excretion), the hyperkalemia risk compounds. This is the same additive-risk logic that will reappear as the "triple whammy" in Session 2.

Class activity (10 minutes): Give groups two or three profiles to teach back in 60 seconds each.

Teaching points: Loops (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide), thiazides (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone), potassium-sparing (spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterene), acetazolamide, mannitol.
